coverage.remaining: None. The 73-page PDF was read in full — all of sections 1-7, every figure caption, every footnote, and the Appendix A table of developers, builders and architects.
coverage.note: Read 73 pages and found 109 address-level facts across 101 distinct number-and-street combinations. The statement has no appendix inventory and no APNs; its addresses come from four seams. Appendix A — the table of developers, builders and architects — is by far the densest, giving a firm, a year and a street number or range for nineteen entries; the photograph captions in §4.7 (property types) and §4.8 (architectural styles) name a building for each type and style; §4.6 dates the district's two schools, its first apartment building and the houses the Marina Corporation's own principals built; and §1 lists the six already-designated or already-identified properties in the district. Where a caption or an Appendix A entry names a row rather than a building — "3253 through 3259 Baker Street", "the bungalows at 14-62 Avila Street" — only the two numbers the source actually prints are recorded, one finding each: the buildings in between are real but their numbers are an inference, and the source twice shows why (it calls 215-287 Avila Street twelve bungalows, a spacing no enumeration would guess, and 2122-2146 Bay Street five). That rule cost the intermediate buildings of 22 rows and is the single biggest reason the yield is 109 rather than several hundred. Never candidates, and so not recorded: three buildings moved out of the city after the fair (605 Woodmont Avenue in Berkeley, 815 Belmont Avenue in Belmont, 1800 5th Avenue in San Rafael); four addresses that appear only inside footnote citations to Planning case records (1410 Jefferson Street, 3440 Baker Street, 465 Marina Boulevard, 2269 Francisco Street), which say nothing about the buildings; and roughly a dozen block-level references with no street number (the forty St. George Holden bungalows on the Baker-Lyon-Francisco-Bay block, Hall & Hamill's 450 feet of Cervantes Boulevard frontage, W. W. Rednall's four houses on the east side of Lyon Street, Meyer Brothers' 1926 six-room flats on Divisadero Street). The statement is thick with the fair's organisers, the Fair heiresses who owned the land and the census analysis of who lived in the district; none of them is recorded. Developers, builders, architects and named firms are recorded in their building role, which the root AGENTS.md privacy limits permit.

notes: The whole 73-page PDF, read end to end. Four cautions. First, Appendix A's table is printed twice in the PDF: Campbell & Hooper, Hall & Hamill, William Staller and Edward A. Janssen each appear in full a second time on the last two pages, with the same text and renumbered footnotes. Read past the repeat rather than treating it as new material. Second, the statement contradicts itself four times and none of the disagreements is adjudicated here: the Marina Branch Library is built in 1953 on p. 41 and 1954 on p. 43; the apartment building at 2250 North Point Street is 1928 under Laurence O. Ebbets and 1929 under Richard R. Irvine; the Sbarboro, Detjen & Jorgensen flats row on Francisco Street is 2225-2255 in the Figure 30 caption and 2229-2269 in Appendix A; and the Marina Safeway is given three addresses — 11 Marina Boulevard on p. 2, 15 Marina Boulevard on p. 33 and 3372 Marina Boulevard on p. 40. Third, the two-column PDF text layer interleaves facing captions, so a regex sweep splices one caption's street onto another's numbers; every caption here was read in the layout, and one of them is mangled at the source — Figure 40 prints "1954-1956 through 1560-1562 Jefferson Street", where the high end has lost its leading 9. Fourth, the Marina district's civic parcels come back from the assessor with a build year of 1900, which is the roll's floor value and not a construction date: Moscone Park, Marina Middle School and Claire Lilienthal School all carry it, and the statement itself warns on p. 40 that 1900 on the roll may stand for something earlier.
